activities.anchor: The ocean is not one body of water but stacked ones
activities.caption: pair each feature with its role in the stack
activities.name: oceanLayerMatch

config.prompt: Pair each feature of the layered ocean with its role:

pairs.right: the sharp density jump sealing the deep warehouse
wind-mixed, holds the oxygen exchange and the phytoplankton
a hot evaporation basin, running saltier than the Atlantic

config.why: The layering is why the ocean's carbon and heat storage work at all — the deep is a warehouse almost sealed from the surface.

activities.anchor: the Bay of Fundy's funnel shape
activities.caption: call the world's largest tide range
activities.name: oceanFundyEst

config.prompt: The Bay of Fundy's funnel shape concentrates its tide into the world's largest range. How big is it?
config.why: A 16-metre range — while enclosed seas like the Mediterranean barely move.
config.context: a three-storey building, twice a day

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the gyres and their edges
activities.name: oceanGyreCloze

config.text: Wind-driven surface currents spin the five great subtropical %%0%% — clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, %%1%% in the Southern. Their %%2%% edges run fast, narrow and deep — the Gulf Stream, the Kuroshio, the Agulhas — while on the %%3%% side, upwelling lifts cold, nutrient-rich water that feeds the world's richest fisheries.
config.hint: The basins' turning wheels; the fast edge is where the boundary current runs, the slow edge is where the deep water comes up.

activities.anchor: In the North Atlantic near Greenland
activities.caption: rebuild the global conveyor's loop
activities.name: oceanConveyorOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the conveyor's journey — what happens first:
items: Surface water cools in winter near Greenland and Antarctica
Salt excluded from forming sea ice makes the brine below denser still — the cold, salty water sinks
It spills southward along the seafloor and spreads through the deep basins of all the oceans
It rises slowly to the surface elsewhere — a round trip of roughly 1,000 years
config.why: A water molecule in the deep ocean may not see daylight again for a millennium — the planet's slow organ of heat and carbon distribution.

activities.anchor: A coast is where the ocean spends its energy
activities.caption: file each landform under the coast that builds it
activities.name: oceanCoastSort

config.prompt: File each landform under the coast that builds it:

items.label: sea caves, arches and stacks in sequence
spits growing past a bay mouth
tombolos tying islands to the mainland

config.why: Erosional coasts are carved where waves hammer; depositional coasts are built where currents drop their load — every landform is a memo from the contest.

activities.anchor: the interventions reliably redistribute the problem
activities.caption: build the groyne — follow the sand
activities.name: oceanGroyneBranch

config.root: Your town's beach is narrowing, so the council builds a groyne perpendicular to the shore.

start.text: The groyne traps longshore drift on its updrift side, and the beach there widens. What happens next?

choices.label: The downdrift beach, starved of sand, erodes faster
choices.feedback: So the next town builds a groyne — and the problem marches down the coast.

choices.label: The sand redistributes evenly along the coast
choices.feedback: Sediment systems are connected end to end — the sand the groyne caught was on its way somewhere.

choices.label: Dredge sand from the downdrift side to feed the updrift
choices.feedback: A wall is always a subsidy taken from somewhere downstream.

march.text: The next town's beach now erodes faster — whose sand was it?

choices.label: Treat the drift as one regional system
choices.feedback: Coastal management is always regional — 'whose sand is this?' is a genuine legal question in several countries.

physics.text: Longshore drift moves metres per day in stormy seasons; walls only decide where it stops.

subsidy.text: The dredge ships the deficit to the next town instead — same ledger, different account.

regional.text: One sediment budget, many towns — the only plan that survives is regional.

config.why: Sediment systems are connected end to end, and a wall is always a subsidy taken from somewhere downstream.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — El Niño arrives off Peru
activities.name: oceanEnsoPredict

config.q: El Niño arrives and the trade winds weaken. What happens to the cold, nutrient-rich upwelling off Peru?
choices: It fails — the warm pool sloshes east and cuts off the nutrient supply, collapsing the fishery
It strengthens — weaker winds stir more deep water up
Nothing changes; the fishery only cares about the seasons
config.why: Peruvian upwelling fails — the name comes from the Christmas-time warm current that killed the anchovy fishery — and the rearranged convection rewrites weather worldwide.

activities.anchor: Water's heat capacity is about four times air's
activities.caption: find the backwards claim — the ocean's numbers
activities.name: oceanMapSpot

config.prompt: One of these ocean numbers is backwards — click it:
lines: The top 3 metres of the ocean store as much heat as the entire atmosphere.
Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid; surface pH has already fallen about 0.1 units.
Sea level rise is measured by satellite altimetry to millimetres.
About three-quarters of the seafloor is mapped to modern resolution.
config.correction: Only about a quarter of the seafloor is mapped to modern resolution — Seabed 2030 is fixing it.
config.why: The planet's largest machine is now instrumented — the Argo fleet profiles it — but its own floor is still mostly blank.
